By the end you will know how to plan small refactor steps, keep tests green, and avoid common mistakes like over‑engineering or forced inheritance. Ready to start refactoring with confidence?

screens.title: Refactoring for SRP: a stepwise approach
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring towards SRP is a process, not a one‑off edit. Start by identifying clusters of methods and data that share a single reason to change. Those clusters are candidates for extraction. Before you change code, ensure you have automated tests that verify the current behavior. If tests are missing, add characterization tests that capture what the class currently does. Then extract one responsibility into a new class, move the methods and the related state, and leave a thin delegating method in the original class. Run the tests and commit. Repeat for the next responsibility. This keeps changes small and reversible. A common concrete pattern is to convert a large service into an orchestrator: the original class delegates validation to an OrderValidator, persistence to an OrderRepository, communication to an EmailService, and so on. Each extracted class should have a focused A P I and minimal knowledge of the orchestrator's internals. A misconception to watch for is treating SRP as an order to make every object tiny; instead, use the reason to change heuristic: group logic that changes for the same reason. After a few small extractions and tests, the system becomes easier to understand and evolve. How would you choose the first responsibility to extract in your codebase?

keyIdea.text: Identify a cohesive responsibility, add tests, extract it, run tests, and commit — repeat until the class is an orchestrator of focused collaborators.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor Workflow
Process
  1. Write or update tests to capture current behavior.
  2. Find a cohesive responsibility using the reason to change heuristic.
  3. Extract a new class and move methods and related state.
  4. Delegate from the original class to the new collaborator.
  5. Run tests and commit small atomic changes.
Common-mistake
Splitting code too finely. If two responsibilities always change together, keep them grouped.
Example: OrderProcessor
Initial responsibility list: validation, persistence, email, inventory updates, invoice generation. Each one is a candidate for extraction.
Key takeaway: Make one extraction at a time and keep tests green.
Check your understanding: Which method group in your services changes most frequently? That is a good first extraction candidate.

screens.title: Extract Class: definition and original example
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Class is the act of selecting a cohesive group of methods and the data they use, then moving them into a new class that has a single responsibility. The original class delegates to the new one. This reduces cognitive load by keeping each class focused and makes unit testing simpler because each class has fewer collaborators. Consider an OrderProcessor that validates orders, saves them, sends emails, updates inventory, and creates invoices. That single class mixes persistence, communication, validation, and reporting responsibilities. The extraction process takes each of those responsibilities — OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, InvoiceGenerator — and creates dedicated classes for them. The original processor becomes an orchestrator whose job is to coordinate these collaborators. A common misconception is that Extract Class always means many tiny classes; instead, extract only when the grouped logic represents a distinct reason to change. For example, validation logic changes when business rules update, while persistence changes when storage choices evolve. Extracting them separates the change surfaces. Try identifying which responsibility in your code changes most often as the first extraction target. Extract Class: definition and original example means move cohesive behavior and data into a new class so both the new class and the original have a single clear responsibility.. In practical terms, what it is and why it reduces responsibility bloat. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Implementing Extract Class: a concrete extraction
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through extracting validation into its own class. First, identify the validation methods and any fields they reference. Create a new class, for example OrderValidator, and move the validation methods there, along with any validation-specific state. Replace the original validation code in OrderProcessor with a call to validator. validate(order). Update the constructor of OrderProcessor to accept an OrderValidator instance so the processor depends on the abstraction of the validator, not on concrete internal code. Run your tests after this change — if tests fail, the failure points are easy to debug because you've made a single focused change. A concrete example: if the original processor had several private methods for checking item availability and customer credit, those belong in OrderValidator. A common misconception is forgetting to move necessary state; make sure any fields used only for validation are relocated with the methods. After extraction, validation logic can be unit tested directly, and the processor's tests can use a simple fake validator. Which validation rule in your codebase would you move first? Implementing Extract Class: a concrete extraction means move methods + state, add a constructor injection for the new class, run tests, and keep the change small and well‑scoped.. In practical terms, move validation out of orderprocessor into ordervalidator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Extract Interface: defining contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Interface creates a narrow contract that callers can depend on instead of concrete implementations. This enables loose coupling and easier testing because implementations can be swapped at runtime. The chapter supplies a canonical example: an IEmailSender interface with a concrete SMTP implementation and a mock used for tests. By depending on the interface, an OrderProcessor or other orchestrator no longer requires a specific email library; during tests you inject a lightweight mock that records calls. When extracting an interface, declare only the methods needed by clients. Avoid adding unrelated operations. A subtle misconception is extracting interfaces too early or with too many methods. Prefer small, purpose‑driven interfaces that reflect a single responsibility. In practice you will: create the interface, update the concrete to implement it, and change dependents to accept the interface via constructor injection. This small step dramatically improves flexibility and supports the Open/Closed Principle as other implementations can be added without changing clients. Extract Interface: defining contracts means an interface defines a minimal contract so different implementations can be swapped without changing callers.. In practical terms, make behavior replaceable and testable with small interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Composition over Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Composition means building objects by assembling other objects that each have a single responsibility. This contrasts with inheritance, which establishes an is‑a relationship and can force subclasses to inherit responsibilities they don't need. The chapter's vehicle example highlights this: if a base class Vehicle exposes a refuel method, ElectricCar may inherit a method that doesn't apply, leading to empty overrides or awkward checks. Instead, compose a Vehicle with a power‑source interface, such as IEngine or IPowerSource, and provide GasolineEngine and ElectricMotor implementations. Composition keeps behavior local to the components that need it, and makes swapping implementations straightforward. A common misconception is that inheritance is always simpler; while inheritance can model true is‑a relationships, it quickly becomes brittle for cross‑cutting concerns like logging, persistence, or communication. Composition combined with small interfaces and dependency injection yields flexible, testable systems. Think about the behaviors in your classes — are they naturally composable, or do they suggest forced inheritance? Composition over Inheritance means compose systems from focused components so you can change behavior by swapping parts instead of changing class hierarchies.. In practical terms, why composing small responsibilities beats deep hierarchies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Composition vs Inheritance
Inheritance Pitfall
Rigid hierarchies force subclasses to share parent responsibilities. Methods that don't apply lead to empty overrides or conditionals.
Example: Vehicle with refuel() that ElectricCar must override blankly.
Composition Pattern
Give Vehicle a power source interface and provide GasolineEngine or ElectricMotor implementations. Swap engines as needed without changing Vehicle logic.
Benefit: Flexible runtime behavior and fewer accidental responsibilities.

screens.title: Dependency Injection: constructor-based composition
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency injection wires collaborators into a class rather than letting the class construct them itself. Constructor injection is the simplest and most explicit form: you add parameters to the constructor for each collaborator and store them as fields. The chapter gives a clear OrderProcessor example that accepts an OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, and InvoiceGenerator in its constructor. This change allows tests to provide mocks or fakes and lets production wiring choose actual implementations. An important safety point is to keep the constructor parameters minimal and consider grouping very small related collaborators behind a facade if the parameter list grows too long. A misconception is thinking DI creates global complexity; instead, DI clarifies boundaries and dependencies. After you extract classes, update consumers to pass the new dependencies, and adjust tests to provide controlled doubles. This approach keeps the orchestration logic pure and easy to verify. Dependency Injection: constructor-based composition means constructor injection exposes dependencies explicitly, enabling easy substitution for testing and flexible production wiring.. In practical terms, make extracted collaborators replaceable and testable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OrderProcessor constructor (from chapter)
public class OrderProcessor {
    private OrderValidator validator;
    private OrderRepository repository;
    private EmailService emailService;
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    private InvoiceGenerator invoiceGenerator;

    public OrderProcessor(OrderValidator validator, OrderRepository repository,
                          EmailService emailService, InventoryService inventoryService,
                          InvoiceGenerator invoiceGenerator) {
        this.validator = validator;
        this.repository = repository;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
        this.invoiceGenerator = invoiceGenerator;
    }

    // processOrder delegates to collaborators
}
This constructor makes dependencies explicit and allows tests to pass mock implementations that simulate behavior without external side effects.

screens.title: Testing and safe refactors
screens.narratorSegment: Tests are the safety net for refactoring. Before extracting a class, ensure you have tests that observe the external behavior of the component you will change. If the tests are missing, add characterization tests that capture what the current implementation does. After extracting a class, write targeted unit tests for the new collaborator and update the original component's tests to use a mock or a fake. Use small commits: one extraction per commit so you can revert a single step if needed. Run the full test suite after each change. Another practical tip is to extract interfaces early for collaborators you want to mock; this simplifies tests and keeps production code decoupled. Finally, avoid over‑engineering: do not create a class for every single small function just because you can. Use the reason to change heuristic to guide granularity. With tests and small steps, refactoring becomes a low‑risk activity that increases code quality over time. Testing and safe refactors means add or update tests before each extraction, keep changes small, and run the suite frequently to prevent regressions.. In practical terms, how to change structure without changing behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Two common anti‑patterns appear during SRP refactors. First, over‑engineering: extracting a new class for tiny bits of logic that always change together increases complexity rather than reducing it. Use the reason to change heuristic — if two behaviors change for the same reason, keep them together. Second, forced inheritance: creating deep hierarchies to share code often leads to subclasses inheriting responsibilities they don't need, resulting in empty methods or convoluted overrides. The vehicle example shows this: forcing ElectricCar to implement a refuel method leads to awkward code. Prefer composition: give Vehicle a power source and inject the appropriate implementation. screens.title: Practical heuristics for splitting responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: When deciding how to split a class, use practical heuristics rather than rigid rules. First, ask the reason to change: if two pieces of logic change together for the same reason, keep them in one class. Second, prefer interfaces for collaborators that represent external systems or side effects, such as email or persistence, because they are natural seams for testing. Third, keep constructor injection explicit but watch parameter bloat; if you find many tiny collaborators, consider grouping them into a small facade. Fourth, always add or update tests before you refactor. Fifth, prefer composition for behavioral differences and inheritance for true is‑a relationships only. Finally, avoid premature extraction: the aim is maintainability, not maximal decomposition. These heuristics will help you balance clarity and simplicity while applying SRP. As you practice, you will get a better instinct for when a split delivers long‑term value and when it just adds ceremony. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to take an existing, messy class and transform it into a set of small, well‑defined components that each have a single reason to change. We focus on three practical moves: extract class to separate responsibilities; extract interface to define clear contracts; and prefer composition over inheritance so responsibilities are composed rather than inherited. You will see concrete Java examples, a hands‑on refactor activity for a user service, and a safe, test‑driven workflow for making incremental changes. This matters because code that follows SRP is easier to test, reason about, and evolve as requirements change. A concrete example you will revisit is an OrderProcessor that initially validates, persists, emails, updates inventory, and generates invoices. We will extract validator, repository, email, inventory, and invoice responsibilities and show how the processor becomes an orchestrator. By the end you will know how to plan small refactor steps, keep tests green, and avoid common mistakes like over‑engineering or forced inheritance. Ready to start refactoring with confidence?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to perform targeted refactors that align code with the Single Responsibility Principle. First, you will master Extract Class and Extract Interface techniques so you can separate validation, persistence, communication, and reporting into their own collaborators. Second, you'll practice transforming a monolithic service into an orchestrator that delegates to focused parts, which improves clarity and testability. Each objective pairs a clear action with why it matters: smaller classes are easier to test, interfaces enable swapping implementations, and composition reduces brittle inheritance chains. For a concrete example, you will refactor a UserService to delegate password hashing and persistence to new components, and you will use an interface to make persistence swappable for tests. These skills let you change one part of the system without rippling effects across unrelated responsibilities, which is the central benefit of SRP.

These objectives emphasize applying the techniques in real code. You will refactor a UserService starter by extracting password hashing and persistence into separate collaborators, and then introduce an interface for persistence so tests can inject a mock. This teaches the interplay between SRP, interfaces, and dependency injection: interfaces define the small contract, and constructor injection composes components at runtime. You will also learn to avoid two common traps. First, don't split code into tiny classes when the logic always changes together; follow the reason to change heuristic. Second, avoid forcing responsibilities into inheritance hierarchies where some subclasses would inherit irrelevant behavior. The exercises and demo reinforce making small, test‑driven steps so you can verify behavior after each extraction. Learning Objectives (continued) means you will be able to refactor a concrete service, create interfaces for testing, and apply composition to simplify evolution.. In practical terms, applied skills and why they matter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Refactoring towards SRP is a process, not a one‑off edit. Start by identifying clusters of methods and data that share a single reason to change. Those clusters are candidates for extraction. Before you change code, ensure you have automated tests that verify the current behavior. If tests are missing, add characterization tests that capture what the class currently does. Then extract one responsibility into a new class, move the methods and the related state, and leave a thin delegating method in the original class. Run the tests and commit. Repeat for the next responsibility. This keeps changes small and reversible. A common concrete pattern is to convert a large service into an orchestrator: the original class delegates validation to an OrderValidator, persistence to an OrderRepository, communication to an EmailService, and so on. Each extracted class should have a focused A P I and minimal knowledge of the orchestrator's internals. A misconception to watch for is treating SRP as an order to make every object tiny; instead, use the reason to change heuristic: group logic that changes for the same reason. After a few small extractions and tests, the system becomes easier to understand and evolve. How would you choose the first responsibility to extract in your codebase?

Extract Class is the act of selecting a cohesive group of methods and the data they use, then moving them into a new class that has a single responsibility. The original class delegates to the new one. This reduces cognitive load by keeping each class focused and makes unit testing simpler because each class has fewer collaborators. Consider an OrderProcessor that validates orders, saves them, sends emails, updates inventory, and creates invoices. That single class mixes persistence, communication, validation, and reporting responsibilities. The extraction process takes each of those responsibilities — OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, InvoiceGenerator — and creates dedicated classes for them. The original processor becomes an orchestrator whose job is to coordinate these collaborators. A common misconception is that Extract Class always means many tiny classes; instead, extract only when the grouped logic represents a distinct reason to change. For example, validation logic changes when business rules update, while persistence changes when storage choices evolve. Extracting them separates the change surfaces. Try identifying which responsibility in your code changes most often as the first extraction target. Extract Class: definition and original example means move cohesive behavior and data into a new class so both the new class and the original have a single clear responsibility.. In practical terms, what it is and why it reduces responsibility bloat. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through extracting validation into its own class. First, identify the validation methods and any fields they reference. Create a new class, for example OrderValidator, and move the validation methods there, along with any validation-specific state. Replace the original validation code in OrderProcessor with a call to validator. validate(order). Update the constructor of OrderProcessor to accept an OrderValidator instance so the processor depends on the abstraction of the validator, not on concrete internal code. Run your tests after this change — if tests fail, the failure points are easy to debug because you've made a single focused change. A concrete example: if the original processor had several private methods for checking item availability and customer credit, those belong in OrderValidator. A common misconception is forgetting to move necessary state; make sure any fields used only for validation are relocated with the methods. After extraction, validation logic can be unit tested directly, and the processor's tests can use a simple fake validator. Which validation rule in your codebase would you move first? Implementing Extract Class: a concrete extraction means move methods + state, add a constructor injection for the new class, run tests, and keep the change small and well‑scoped.. In practical terms, move validation out of orderprocessor into ordervalidator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Extract Interface creates a narrow contract that callers can depend on instead of concrete implementations. This enables loose coupling and easier testing because implementations can be swapped at runtime. The chapter supplies a canonical example: an IEmailSender interface with a concrete SMTP implementation and a mock used for tests. By depending on the interface, an OrderProcessor or other orchestrator no longer requires a specific email library; during tests you inject a lightweight mock that records calls. When extracting an interface, declare only the methods needed by clients. Avoid adding unrelated operations. A subtle misconception is extracting interfaces too early or with too many methods. Prefer small, purpose‑driven interfaces that reflect a single responsibility. In practice you will: create the interface, update the concrete to implement it, and change dependents to accept the interface via constructor injection. This small step dramatically improves flexibility and supports the Open/Closed Principle as other implementations can be added without changing clients. Extract Interface: defining contracts means an interface defines a minimal contract so different implementations can be swapped without changing callers.. In practical terms, make behavior replaceable and testable with small interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Composition means building objects by assembling other objects that each have a single responsibility. This contrasts with inheritance, which establishes an is‑a relationship and can force subclasses to inherit responsibilities they don't need. The chapter's vehicle example highlights this: if a base class Vehicle exposes a refuel method, ElectricCar may inherit a method that doesn't apply, leading to empty overrides or awkward checks. Instead, compose a Vehicle with a power‑source interface, such as IEngine or IPowerSource, and provide GasolineEngine and ElectricMotor implementations. Composition keeps behavior local to the components that need it, and makes swapping implementations straightforward. A common misconception is that inheritance is always simpler; while inheritance can model true is‑a relationships, it quickly becomes brittle for cross‑cutting concerns like logging, persistence, or communication. Composition combined with small interfaces and dependency injection yields flexible, testable systems. Think about the behaviors in your classes — are they naturally composable, or do they suggest forced inheritance? Composition over Inheritance means compose systems from focused components so you can change behavior by swapping parts instead of changing class hierarchies.. In practical terms, why composing small responsibilities beats deep hierarchies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dependency injection wires collaborators into a class rather than letting the class construct them itself. Constructor injection is the simplest and most explicit form: you add parameters to the constructor for each collaborator and store them as fields. The chapter gives a clear OrderProcessor example that accepts an OrderValidator, OrderRepository, EmailService, InventoryService, and InvoiceGenerator in its constructor. This change allows tests to provide mocks or fakes and lets production wiring choose actual implementations. An important safety point is to keep the constructor parameters minimal and consider grouping very small related collaborators behind a facade if the parameter list grows too long. A misconception is thinking DI creates global complexity; instead, DI clarifies boundaries and dependencies. After you extract classes, update consumers to pass the new dependencies, and adjust tests to provide controlled doubles. This approach keeps the orchestration logic pure and easy to verify. Dependency Injection: constructor-based composition means constructor injection exposes dependencies explicitly, enabling easy substitution for testing and flexible production wiring.. In practical terms, make extracted collaborators replaceable and testable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tests are the safety net for refactoring. Before extracting a class, ensure you have tests that observe the external behavior of the component you will change. If the tests are missing, add characterization tests that capture what the current implementation does. After extracting a class, write targeted unit tests for the new collaborator and update the original component's tests to use a mock or a fake. Use small commits: one extraction per commit so you can revert a single step if needed. Run the full test suite after each change. Another practical tip is to extract interfaces early for collaborators you want to mock; this simplifies tests and keeps production code decoupled. Finally, avoid over‑engineering: do not create a class for every single small function just because you can. Use the reason to change heuristic to guide granularity. With tests and small steps, refactoring becomes a low‑risk activity that increases code quality over time. Two common anti‑patterns appear during SRP refactors. First, over‑engineering: extracting a new class for tiny bits of logic that always change together increases complexity rather than reducing it. Use the reason to change heuristic — if two behaviors change for the same reason, keep them together. When deciding how to split a class, use practical heuristics rather than rigid rules. First, ask the reason to change: if two pieces of logic change together for the same reason, keep them in one class. Second, prefer interfaces for collaborators that represent external systems or side effects, such as email or persistence, because they are natural seams for testing. Third, keep constructor injection explicit but watch parameter bloat; if you find many tiny collaborators, consider grouping them into a small facade. Fourth, always add or update tests before you refactor. Fifth, prefer composition for behavioral differences and inheritance for true is‑a relationships only. Finally, avoid premature extraction: the aim is maintainability, not maximal decomposition. These heuristics will help you balance clarity and simplicity while applying SRP.
